preview.scannerButton: Push button: click next view, double-click scan, hold auto-scan
preview.scannerCaption: Example networks and addresses, not yours. Click = next view, double-click = scan now, hold 0.6 s = auto-scan on/off. “{{join}}” shows what joining looks like. Your board shows the real networks around you.

phone.caption: The board on the left of this page shows the LED colour too. Your real board does all of this over Wi-Fi.

weather.screen: Simulated weather and oracle screen, example data
weather.button: Push button: click next view, double-click refresh or new haiku
weather.caption: Example city, weather and oracle answers, not live. Click = next view, double-click = refresh (oracle view: a new haiku). Your board shows your city and real answers from the model you pick.

scan.goal: The radio visits each 2.4 GHz channel in turn, asks “who's there?” (a probe request) and listens for replies and for the beacons every router sends about 10 times a second. A full pass takes 2–3 seconds.
scan.channels: Channels 1 to 13, the one being scanned is highlighted
scan.channelClean: Channel {{channel}} · one of the three that don't overlap
scan.caption: dBm is logarithmic: every 3 dB less means half the power. −90 is a million times weaker than −30.

web.drawingAlt: The phone talks to the board directly. The React app talks to the Node server, which talks to the board. The board pushes live updates back over WebSockets.

rows.status: what the board is doing; last scan
rows.led: LED colour; text on the screen
rows.wifi: save a network (open during set-up, <adm>admin</adm> after)
rows.ws: pushes status every second, scans, button presses, update progress

remote.drawingAlt: Your phone reaches the tunnel's public address over HTTPS. Your Mac and the board both dial out to the tunnel, so nothing is opened on your router. The tunnel hands the phone's requests and the board's connection to the Node server on your Mac.
remote.home: your home · router: nothing opened, nothing forwarded
remote.caption: Hosted server instead of a tunnel? The Node server runs there (VPS, Fly.io, Render…) behind its HTTPS, and the board dials straight to it: the tunnel and your Mac drop out. Same firmware, same relay wss://….

W1.title: Scan & join
W1.capability: scanner views, join your network, password stored on the chip, reconnects by itself, status view with clock, IP and signal chart, bench.local

W2.title: Phone control
W2.capability: REST API + WebSocket, phone page at bench.local, set-up network, firmware updates over HTTP, React + Node dashboard on your Mac

W3.title: Internet & AI
W3.capability: HTTPS + JSON from the internet (Open-Meteo weather); the Bench Oracle: any AI model through a LiteLLM gateway, answers as structured JSON
W3.needs: W1 + the LiteLLM gateway and a provider key for the oracle

W4.title: Radio lab (bonus)
W4.capability: channel activity from packet counts; board-to-board messages with ESP-NOW

W5.title: Hardware Diary
W5.capability: post bench entries and photos of your builds to this repo's API

roadmap.caption: Each lab has its own firmware and command (wifi-lab-w1, wifi-lab-w2, …); what they share lives in kit/lib/wifi-kit, so each lab adds features instead of starting over.

job.title: loop() hands over a job
job.text: Every 15 minutes (or on a double-click) loop() puts one job in the worker's mailbox, then goes straight back to drawing. It never waits for the network.

connect.title: Find the server and connect
connect.text: DNS turns the name into an IP address, then the board opens a TCP connection to port 443, the HTTPS port.

tls.title: TLS: is it really Open-Meteo?
tls.text: The server sends its certificate. The board checks that it chains up to one of the root certificates built into the firmware, and that it was issued for this name. Then both sides agree on encryption keys: from here on, nobody in between can read or change the data.

get.title: Ask for the forecast
get.text: One GET request with the coordinates and the list of values we want: now, the next 24 hours, 7 days.

json.title: The answer: JSON
json.text: About 1.7 KB of text in JSON. Almost a third of it is time stamps the screen never shows.

filter.title: Keep only what we draw
filter.text: An ArduinoJson filter is a stencil: fields not in it are skipped while reading, so they never take memory.

back.title: Hand the result back
back.text: The worker puts a small struct in the mailbox (under a mutex, so the two tasks never touch it at the same time) and bumps a version number.

draw.title: The next frame shows it
draw.text: loop() sees the new version, copies the struct, and the next frame draws the new sky. The frame counter on the left never stopped.

job.title: loop() describes the moment
job.text: loop() writes what the board knows as a small JSON text and hands it to the worker with the gateway address, its key and the model name.

request.title: One standard request
request.text: The board always sends the same OpenAI-style request, whatever model is behind it. It offers one function, show_on_bench, and forces the model to call it.

route.title: LiteLLM picks the real model
route.text: config.yaml maps the name the board asked for to a provider and model, and adds that provider's key from .env. Change the mapping and the board uses another model, no reflash.

translate.title: Translated for the provider
translate.text: LiteLLM rewrites the request in the provider's own format (for Anthropic: the Messages API with a forced tool) and sends it over HTTPS.

writing.title: The model writes
writing.text: A few seconds. The worker task waits on the network; loop() does not: watch the frame counter keep running while the screen keeps animating.

call.title: An answer in the agreed shape
call.text: Because the function was forced, the answer is not free text: it is a call to show_on_bench with JSON arguments.

standard.title: Back in the standard format
standard.text: LiteLLM turns the provider's answer back into the OpenAI format, so the board parses one shape for every provider. Token counts come along.

parse.title: JSON inside JSON
parse.text: The arguments arrive as a JSON string inside the JSON answer, so the board parses twice. Then it folds the text to plain ASCII (the screen fonts have no é or —) and turns #5fa8ff into red, green, blue.

show.title: Screen and LED
show.text: loop() picks up the answer: the title in its colour, the lines typed out, the LED lit, time and tokens underneath.
